newsitem.title: USA: Oil, grains weakness keeps pressure on commodities.
newsitem.headline: Oil, grains weakness keeps pressure on commodities.

text.p: Crude oil prices ended lower for the fifth straight day on Friday as bearish sentiment tightened its hold on a market shaken by steep losses this week.

In other markets, grains fell and metals were mixed as investors continued to exit commodities in favour of stocks and bonds after U.S. economic data this week suggested slow growth, low inflation and little chance of higher interest rates.
The selling pushed the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau's index of 17 futures down another 0.53 point at 237.30, a 12-month low. The index fell 3.83 points Thursday.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices continued their fall from last year's six-year highs as worries about historically low heating oil supplies faded.
December crude oil fell 32 cents a barrel at $23.03. The benchmark contract ended down $1.83 or 7.4 percent for the week.
"People are still a bit shell-shocked and nobody seems to want to buy crude with this new bearish market," said Al Lindseth, a trader with GSC Energy in Atlanta.

A buildup in heating oil stocks the last two weeks had already fed selling when news of an extended ceasefire among Kurdish factions on Thursday prompted speculators to exit the market on ideas that the deal might lead to Iraqi oil sales.
Crude's losses weighed on December heating oil, which ended down 0.25 cent at 66.60 cents a gallon. But December gasoline ended up 0.09 cent at 64.70 cents a gallon on low stockpiles.
"Gasoline fundamentals are good given the inventory situation and refinery turnarounds," said Smith Barney analyst John Saucer.

Gasoline inventories are 10.7 million barrels below year ago, putting stocks at 20-year lows, traders said. With refineries undergoing seasonal maintenance and maximizing distillate or heating oil production ahead of winter, gasoline stocks are not seen rebuilding significantly soon.

Disagreement between the United States and Iraq continues to put on ice a deal under which certain United Nations sanctions would be lifted against Iraq to enable it to sell $2 billion worth of oil in exchange for food and humanitarian supplies.
But crude oil was unable to strengthen when U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Madeleine Albright on Friday said Iraq was making "outrageous demands" on how the deal must be implemented.
"As an example of the bearish sentiment, we got no response out of Madeleine Albright growling at Iraq," said Tim Evans, an analyst with Pegasus Econometric Group.
The U.N. Security Council voted at its regular 60-day review to hold in place broad sanctions against Iraq placed after the Gulf War six years ago.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, most grain prices continued to fall as optimism about this year's corn and soybean crops now being harvested grew. Clear harvest weather also added selling.
November soybeans closed 4-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $6.63-1/4, its lowest level since November 1995. New life of contract lows were also set in soymeal and soyoil markets.
December corn ended down 3 cents at $2.63, a 14-month low.
Meteorologists said U.S. Midwest soybean producers would experience a cold weekend but warmer weather was expected next week amid generally dry conditions.
"Good harvest weather all weekend weighed on corn and weakness in beans weighed on corn," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds.
At the COMEX division of the New York Mercantile Exchange, metals prices ended mixed as the market steadied after Thursday's selloff by inflation-conscious investment funds.

"You'd have to say the longer term trend was still down, with any lack of momentum today not surprising on a Friday, and support in gold probably somewhere down in the low $370's," Imperial Bank's chief bullion dealer Jeff Singer said.
December gold ended up 10 cents at $379.20 an ounce, after trading in a $379.50-377.80 range and December silver closed down 1.0 cent at $4.798.
U.S. economic data released Friday, including October non-farm payrolls, October unemployment, and September leading indicators, suggested inflation remained little threat.
Meanwhile the strength of the U.S. dollar, which saw a 42 month high gainst the yen this week, was depressing demand for precious metals in jewelry and industry in Japan, analysts said.
